result.target_topic: Proposed and Adopted AML/CFT Rule Changes for Investment Advisers
result.target_summary: In 2024, FinCEN and the SEC proposed rules requiring investment advisers to implement procedures to identify and verify customer identities, and FinCEN proposed amendments to BSA program requirements including periodic risk assessments. Additionally, FinCEN adopted a rule effective January 1, 2026, including certain investment advisers in the definition of 'financial institutions' under BSA rules, prescribing minimum AML/CFT program standards and suspicious activity reporting obligations.

target_year_over_year_context.explanation: This is a many-to-many split. D156 (2023) covers the AMLA broadly: reforming/modernizing BSA, risk-based approach, Treasury priorities, enforcement expansion, whistleblower protections, and FinCEN priorities. In 2024, this broad AMLA topic is split into multiple disclosures: D150 covers the consolidated BSA/AMLA framework; D151 covers the AMLA impact depending on rulemaking and FinCEN priorities; D152 covers the Corporate Transparency Act (enacted as part of AMLA); D153 covers specific proposed/adopted rules for investment advisers under AMLA/BSA. Each 2024 disclosure addresses a specific sub-topic introduced or contained within D156. We provide separate rows for the logical links: D156->D151 (AMLA impact/priorities), D156->D152 (AMLA/CTA), D156->D153 (AMLA/Investment Adviser rules), and D156->D150 (AMLA/BSA framework). Note: D150 is also linked from D155. This is allowed as separate rows.

current_disclosures.section: Regulation > Anti-Money Laundering and Anti-Bribery Rules and Regulations
current_disclosures.summary: The U.S. Bank Secrecy Act (BSA), as amended by the USA PATRIOT Act and the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 (AMLA), establishes anti-money laundering and financial transparency laws requiring client identification, transaction monitoring, and suspicious activity reporting. The AMLA comprehensively reformed these laws by codifying a risk-based compliance approach, expanding enforcement authorities and sanctions, and requiring Treasury to set priorities and test standards.

current_disclosures.section: Regulation > Anti-Money Laundering and Anti-Bribery Rules and Regulations
current_disclosures.summary: The impact of the AMLA depends on additional rulemakings and implementation guidance, though the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has already issued required anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism priorities. These priorities include corruption, cybercrime, terrorist financing, fraud, transnational crime, drug trafficking, human trafficking, and proliferation financing.

current_disclosures.section: Regulation > Anti-Money Laundering and Anti-Bribery Rules and Regulations
current_disclosures.summary: The Corporate Transparency Act (CTA), enacted in 2021 as part of the AMLA, established beneficial ownership information reporting requirements implemented by a FinCEN rule effective in 2024. Domestic companies formed before 2024 must file initial reports by January 1, 2025 (later announced as March 21, 2025), while those formed in or after 2024 must file within 90 or 30 days of formation, subject to exemptions.

comparisons.peer_summary: The Corporation is subject to LRRs regarding bribery, corruption, know-your-customer requirements, anti-money laundering, embargoes, and sanctions. This includes the U.S. Bank Secrecy Act, OFAC sanctions programs, the FCPA, and the U.K. Bribery Act. In 2024, federal regulators proposed amendments to update AML program requirements for supervised institutions.
comparisons.comparison: Both Goldman Sachs and Bank of America disclose that in 2024, federal regulators proposed amendments to update Anti-Money Laundering (AML) program requirements for supervised financial institutions, specifically focusing on the identification, evaluation, and documentation of money laundering risks. However, Goldman Sachs specifically highlights a parallel proposal from the SEC and FinCEN targeting investment advisers to implement customer identity verification procedures, and notes the adoption of a rule effective Jan 1, 2026, that explicitly includes certain investment advisers (like itself) in the definition of 'financial institutions' under BSA rules, prescribing minimum program standards and suspicious activity reporting obligations. Bank of America's disclosure focuses more broadly on the regulatory framework (BSA, OFAC, FCPA) and the proposed amendments for supervised institutions generally, without mentioning the specific expansion of AML obligations to investment advisers as a distinct 2024 event or the Jan 2026 effective date.

sentences.text: In 2024, FinCEN and the SEC proposed a rule that would require certain investment advisers to implement reasonable procedures to identify and verify the identities of their customers.

In 2024, FinCEN proposed to amend the anti-money laundering/countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) program requirements for all financial institutions subject to the BSA that have AML/CFT program obligations, including us.

FinCEN has also adopted a rule, effective on January 1, 2026, that includes certain investment advisers, such as us, in the definition of "financial institutions" under FinCEN's rules implementing the BSA and, among other things, prescribes minimum standards for AML/CFT programs to be established by such investment advisers and requires them to report suspicious activity to FinCEN.

The Corporation is also subject to extensive LRRs in the U.S. and in the other jurisdictions in which it operates regarding bribery and corruption, know-your-customer requirements, anti-money laundering, embargo programs and economic sanctions.

In 2024, federal regulators, including the Federal Reserve and the OCC, proposed amendments to update the requirements for supervised institutions to establish, implement and maintain effective, risk-based and reasonably designed anti-money laundering programs, including the identification, evaluation and documentation of money laundering risks.

comparisons.peer_topic: BSA internal controls and reporting requirements
comparisons.peer_summary: The Bank Secrecy Act requires financial institutions to establish risk-based internal controls to prevent money laundering and terrorism financing, alongside record-keeping, reporting, and due diligence obligations.
comparisons.comparison: Both Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase identify the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) as the foundational statute imposing AML obligations on financial institutions, including risk-based internal controls, record-keeping, and reporting. A key difference is that Goldman Sachs' 2024 disclosure emphasizes new regulatory *changes* and *proposals*, specifically the adoption of a rule in 2024 effective in 2026 that expands the definition of 'financial institutions' to include certain investment advisers like GS, and proposed rules for customer identity verification. In contrast, JPMorgan's 2024 disclosure describes the existing statutory requirements of the BSA for financial institutions and broker-dealers without highlighting specific new 2024 rulemakings that expand the scope of AML obligations to investment advisers.

sentences.text: FinCEN has also adopted a rule, effective on January 1, 2026, that includes certain investment advisers, such as us, in the definition of "financial institutions" under FinCEN's rules implementing the BSA and, among other things, prescribes minimum standards for AML/CFT programs to be established by such investment advisers and requires them to report suspicious activity to FinCEN.

In 2024, FinCEN proposed to amend the anti-money laundering/countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) program requirements for all financial institutions subject to the BSA that have AML/CFT program obligations, including us.

The Bank Secrecy Act ("BSA") requires all financial institutions, including banks and securities broker-dealers, to establish a risk-based system of internal controls reasonably designed to prevent money laundering and the financing of terrorism.
The BSA includes a variety of record-keeping and reporting requirements, as well as due diligence/know-your-customer documentation requirements.

comparisons.peer_summary: In the U.S., the Bank Secrecy Act, as amended, imposes significant obligations on financial institutions to detect and deter money laundering and terrorist financing, including requirements to develop AML programs, verify customer identity, and monitor and report suspicious activity.
comparisons.comparison: Both Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley disclose that the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) imposes significant obligations on financial institutions to detect and deter money laundering and terrorist financing, including requirements to develop AML programs and verify customer identity. A specific point of convergence is the requirement for identity verification, which Goldman Sachs links to a specific 2024 SEC/FinCEN proposal for investment advisers. Morgan Stanley's disclosure is broader, stating that the BSA (as amended by PATRIOT and AMLA) imposes these obligations on banks, broker-dealers, and others, but does not detail the specific 2024 regulatory proposals or the 2026 rule adoption that Goldman Sachs highlights regarding the inclusion of investment advisers in BSA 'financial institution' definitions.

sentences.text: In 2024, FinCEN and the SEC proposed a rule that would require certain investment advisers to implement reasonable procedures to identify and verify the identities of their customers.

FinCEN has also adopted a rule, effective on January 1, 2026, that includes certain investment advisers, such as us, in the definition of "financial institutions" under FinCEN's rules implementing the BSA and, among other things, prescribes minimum standards for AML/CFT programs to be established by such investment advisers and requires them to report suspicious activity to FinCEN.

In the U.S., the Bank Secrecy Act, as amended by the USA PATRIOT Act of 2001 and the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020, imposes significant obligations on financial institutions to detect and deter money laundering and terrorist financing activity, including requiring banks, broker-dealers, futures commission merchants, introducing brokers and mutual funds to develop and implement AML programs, verify the identity of customers that maintain accounts, and monitor and report suspicious activity to appropriate law enforcement or regulatory authorities.
